content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines and recommendations regarding the elimination of leprosy as a public health problem and the interruption of its transmission. These guidelines emphasize that countries may copy, adapt, and redistribute the work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons license. If translations are created, a disclaimer must be included, stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation. The WHO has established a Task Force on Definitions, Criteria, and Indicators for the Interruption of Transmission and Elimination of Leprosy (TFCEL). This task force was created to define practical criteria for assessing the interruption of leprosy transmission and its elimination as a disease. The task force has developed frameworks, definitions, and verification processes to guide countries in achieving these milestones. The work includes drafting definitions, identifying criteria for different phases of leprosy control, and creating templates for country dossiers to document progress. Leprosy elimination as a public health problem has been achieved in most countries, with many reporting zero new cases in recent years. The WHO's roadmap for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and the Global Leprosy Strategy 2021–2030 aim to achieve zero new autochthonous leprosy cases in 120 countries by 2030. Verification of this achievement may involve submitting a dossier and undergoing independent review. The task force has held multiple meetings, including a final meeting in Chengalpattu, India, in March 2021, to finalize criteria for defining the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy. The meeting also aimed to recommend a template for country dossiers and propose verification exercises. The task force's work has been informed by lessons learned from other diseases and includes the development of indicators, protocols, and guidelines for assessing progress. The elimination of leprosy involves several phases: achieving elimination as a public health problem, interrupting transmission, and ultimately eliminating the disease. Due to the long incubation period of leprosy, there may be a significant time gap between these phases. The task force has proposed definitions and indicators for each phase, including the absence of new autochthonous child cases for at least three consecutive years as a proxy for transmission interruption. Migration has been identified as a key challenge in leprosy elimination, particularly in India, where internal migration affects 29% of the population. A pilot project by FAIRMED India, in partnership with Novartis, is studying the impact of migration on leprosy patients and its consequences for treatment and health-seeking behavior. The project aims to provide evidence-based recommendations for managing leprosy in the context of migration. The WHO has also outlined definitions for control, elimination, and eradication of diseases. Control refers to reducing disease incidence and prevalence to acceptable levels, while elimination as a public health problem involves achieving measurable global targets. Elimination of transmission refers to reducing infection incidence to zero in a defined area, and elimination of disease involves zero new autochthonous cases for at least three consecutive years. Eradication, which is not currently applicable to leprosy due to zoonotic transmission pathways, refers to the permanent reduction of a pathogen to zero globally. The task force has developed a draft framework for defining and verifying the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy. This includes criteria for readiness to move to the next phase, indicators for assessing progress, and protocols for testing and piloting potential indicators. The task force has also emphasized the importance of continued surveillance and monitoring to sustain progress and prevent reintroduction of the disease.
